Welcome to Nanoscience!

Welcome, everybody! I am so glad you all made it. I have to apologize for the mix-up this morning—it turns out I put down three different venues for this class on Canvas. But you found us! We are in Williams Hall, Room 320.

This is actually my tenth year teaching here at Virginia Tech, and this is the first time I think I have ever botched the classroom location on the first day. But I will have you know that I am a human being. Just like ChatGPT, I will make mistakes! It is your job to keep me accountable. If something seems a little off, or you are not sure about a detail, please ask me.

First days can be a little nerve-wracking. To shake off the nerves and get out of those cramped airplane-style chairs, we started our session today by standing up, spreading out, and doing some physical stretches. Remember to breathe, stretch those arms, and make some funny noises if you need to! For the next 45 minutes, you are stuck in this room, so we might as well get comfortable.

Meet Coach Emori

I am Dr. Satoru Emori. You can call me Dr. Emori, Professor Emori, or even Coach Emori. I actually prefer “Coach” because it conveys a specific message: we are going to do things a little differently in this class.

Whenever possible, we will actively do stuff. Yes, at times you will have to hear me blabber on about nanoscience concepts, but my main job is to get you engaged, working with your hands, and hopefully hooked on the subject. Nanoscience is a highly interdisciplinary field. My own background is in materials science and physics—specifically researching magnetic materials used for digital memory storage in cloud data centers. But nanoscience encompasses so much more.

You are stuck with me for the first four weeks. After that, we have a wonderful lineup of guest instructors coming in with expertise ranging from computational biology to nanomedicine, environmental geoscience, and quantum phenomena. They will give you a broad overview of everything that falls under the nanoscience umbrella.

Course Philosophy and Ground Rules

This class is a fantastic opportunity to get to know your fellow classmates. If you are a nanoscience or nanomedicine major, research is a required component of your degree, and you might end up working in labs with the very people sitting next to you. To help facilitate this, I will shuffle your seating a few times throughout the semester.

To keep things running smoothly, we have two simple ground rules:

  • We are all here to learn, and we help each other out. That includes me! My learning experience started this morning when I realized I need to double-check my Canvas location posts. The goal here is not to show off who knows more. We are a team.

  • Stash the screens. I love seeing laptops closed and phones put away. Keep your electronics stashed unless you are explicitly told to take them out for a specific class activity.

Logistics: The Weekly Rhythm

You are in college, which means you have to do some work to get credit and graduate. For the first few weeks, you can expect a short homework assignment after every single class. These are meant to be straightforward and manageable.

Our default deadline for homework is 9:00 AM on the day of our next class. Since our class starts at 10:10 AM, that means your homework is due exactly 70 minutes before we meet.

As shown in the schedule above, I will host optional office hours on Wednesdays and Thursdays from 2:15 PM to 3:15 PM. Note the location carefully: we will be in ICTAS II, 1st-floor Conference Room 164. People have had trouble finding this building in the past, so use Google Maps if you need to!

Friday Quizzes

For the first four weeks, every Friday will feature an in-class quiz. Here is what you need to know about the format for Quiz 1:

  • It will be taken in class.

  • Expected completion time is under 10 minutes (though you will have about 20 minutes allotted).

  • No collaboration with neighbors, no calculators, no cheat sheets, and no electronics.

Quiz 1 Hints: You will be tested on syllabus items (highlighted in yellow on the document) and your intuition for length scales. You need to know the approximate values of various objects, choosing from options ranging from \sim 10\text{ m} down to \sim 0.1\text{ nm}.

Start building your mental ruler for these scales:

  • Macro scale: Width of our classroom (\sim 10\text{ m}), height of a human (\sim 1\text{ m}), diameter of an apple (\sim 10\text{ cm} or 100\text{ mm}), and the width of a human fingernail plate (\sim 1\text{ cm} or 10\text{ mm}).

  • Milli/Micro scale: Width of a sesame seed (\sim 1\text{ mm}), width of a human hair (\sim 100\ \mu\text{m}), diameter of a human red blood cell (\sim 10\ \mu\text{m}), thickness of a human red blood cell (\sim 1\ \mu\text{m}), and the length of an E-coli bacterium (\sim 1\ \mu\text{m}).

  • Nano scale: Diameter of a SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) virus (\sim 100\text{ nm}), lipid bilayer thickness (\sim 10\text{ nm}), diameter of a carbon buckyball (\sim 1\text{ nm}), and the diameter of a typical atom (\sim 0.1\text{ nm} or 1\text{ angstrom}).

Learning is a Physical Act

During class, we did a quick icebreaker where you made name tags and chatted with your neighbors. I walked around and asked some of you about your hobbies. We talked about sports, music, and training. Why did I ask about that? Because it ties directly into how we learn.

Let’s talk about Jacob Misiorowski. He is currently one of the best pitching prospects in baseball, known for throwing a fastball at over 100 miles per hour. I want to throw 100 mph too! So, I did what anyone in 2026 would do: I asked ChatGPT how to move my body like Jacob Misiorowski.

ChatGPT gave me a great, concise, step-by-step breakdown of the mechanics. Leg drive, front-leg brace, hips first, torso follows, arm stays loose, release, and finish. I have a PhD; I know how to read. So, by simply reading and following these step-by-step instructions, I should be able to step on a mound today and pitch 100 mph, right?

When I asked the class this, you all immediately disagreed with me. And you were right.

I don’t have the foundational strength, the flexibility, or the fast-twitch muscle memory required. Misiorowski trained for years to build the physical capacity to execute those mechanics. Furthermore, ChatGPT’s instructions are generic and might not even fit my specific body type. Even though it is sad to admit that I won’t be striking out my little-leaguer son with a flaming fastball anytime soon, reading instructions is not a substitute for physical training.

Learning STEM is exactly the same way.

Me reading a short ChatGPT prompt and expecting to throw 100 mph is just like a student expecting to ace a quiz, crush an exam, or be effective at a technical job just by reading a textbook or glancing at lecture slides the night before.

Learning is a physical act. When you practice, you are literally building and strengthening physical neural connections in your brain. Without consistent practice and training, your brain simply will not have the “muscle” to solve complex problems. If you try to perform without putting in the reps, you end up throwing the academic equivalent of an embarrassing ceremonial first pitch.

Building Foundation: SI Prefixes

To avoid throwing wild pitches in nanoscience, we have to build our foundational strength. In this class, that means internalizing the standard SI prefixes and their associated scientific notation.

You must know these prefixes from Giga- (10^9) down to pico- (10^{-12}) by our quiz on Friday. Notice that we crossed out hecto, deka, and deci—we rarely use those in standard scientific engineering contexts. We operate in powers of three (thousands, millions, billions).

How do you build the physical brain connections to memorize these? We discussed a few strategies in class:

  • Old-fashioned flashcards: Tried, tested, and highly effective for rote memorization.

  • AI-generated quizzes: You can prompt an AI to generate rapid-fire conversion questions for you to practice.

  • Physical associations: Connect these abstract numbers to the real-world objects we discussed earlier (like associating 100\ \mu\text{m} with a human hair, or 0.1\text{ nm} with an atom). Grounding the math in physical reality helps the concepts stick.

Keep working at it until it becomes second nature. The homework due Wednesday morning is designed to give you those necessary repetitions.

Hands-On: The Mystery Crystal

We wrapped up our first day by getting our hands dirty. Everyone received a “goodie bag” containing a diamond scribe and a small, flat “mystery crystal.”

Your task was to try and cut the crystal using the scribe. As you quickly discovered, it is not as easy as it looks! The room was filled with unpleasant, squeaky scratching sounds and a whole lot of shattering rather than clean, straight cuts.

I heard some great guesses about what the material might be—common theories included various metal alloys or graphite. I won’t spoil the answer just yet. On Wednesday, I will reveal exactly what this mystery crystal is, and more importantly, I will demonstrate the proper technique to cut it cleanly like a pro.

See you all on Wednesday. Remember to submit your homework by 9:00 AM!
